ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial academic-video-call feel, with mostly short to medium turns during setup and discussion, but long, highly structured presentation turns from speakers. Early conversation is loose and overlapping, full of greetings, side comments, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “right”), and occasional technical-check interruptions. Speakers use frequent hedging and self-repair—“I think,” “sort of,” “you know,” “maybe,” “I mean,” “I guess”—especially when speculating or answering questions. Formality rises during introductions and talks, though even there delivery remains conversational, with false starts, repetitions, filler words, and audience-oriented signposting. Questions are generally polite and prefaced with praise or disclaimers such as “quick question,” “naive question,” or “great talk,” then unfold in multi-part, exploratory form. Challenges are indirect and collaborative: participants frame alternatives as possibilities, ask for clarification, and build on prior answers rather than openly contradicting. Responses often begin with agreement or appreciation, then qualify the answer, acknowledge limitations, and identify open questions.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - This might be a dumb question, but is that normal for this kind of data?
  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start mid-thought, as if the conversation was already under way before the recording started.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Protecting outdoor workers from wildfire smoke when air-quality alerts arrive after the shift has already started.

speakers.name: Maya Chen
speakers.background: Fourth-year PhD candidate in environmental exposure science with prior field experience supporting wildfire-smoke monitoring campaigns in agricultural valleys and suburban construction corridors. She works with regulatory PM2.5 networks, low-cost sensor calibration, satellite smoke products, and plume forecasts, and has built reproducible pipelines that align air-quality data with worksite geography and shift schedules. She is responsible for the pilot's environmental data linkage and quality-control protocol.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats exposure-time assignment as a measurement-validity and reproducibility problem. She favors an operational county-level trigger based on the earliest official alert issuance or pre-specified exceedance at the nearest regulatory monitor during a shift, with forecast data retained as secondary descriptive context. In her view, this creates an independently verifiable timestamp that can be applied consistently across occupations and worksites, including workers whose employers do not share records. She is concerned that relying primarily on recalled receipt or incomplete workplace documentation would introduce differential recall, missingness, and retrospective reconstruction of the exposure event.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
speakers.background: Research engineer with 11 years of experience designing occupational and environmental-health studies, including mobile-worker cohorts and rapid-response data collection after heat and air-quality events. His work combines time-varying exposure assignment, SMS and survey instruments, GPS-informed work-location histories, and causal diagrams to distinguish environmental hazards from workplace interventions. He will lead the pilot's analytic data architecture and participant follow-up procedures.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Rafael frames the central exposure as the intervention pathway: whether and when a worker actually receives a warning and has an opportunity to respond. He advocates defining the primary alert-exposure time as participant-reported receipt of an alert or supervisor communication, corroborated by message logs when available, then assessing a short window using actual work location and task. He argues that a county-level trigger can classify people as alerted when they never received a message, were working indoors, had changed locations or tasks, or were already using protections. His concern is intervention misclassification: a clean environmental timestamp may not represent the warning process the study is meant to evaluate.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Lucía Benítez
speakers.background: Labor sociologist with 16 years of community-engaged research on contingent work, immigrant worker networks, and workplace health communication in agriculture, landscaping, logistics, and construction. She uses multilingual interviews, participant observation, organizational network mapping, and worker-led advisory groups. Her recent work has examined how workers weigh safety decisions against lost wages, retaliation concerns, and unstable scheduling.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Lucía focuses on how alerts travel through unequal employment relationships rather than assuming a single official communication channel. She will press the team to document whether information came from supervisors, coworkers, family, Spanish-language media and messaging networks, worker organizations, or not at all, along with workers' concerns about losing shifts or being viewed as difficult. She does not claim authority over the environmental or epidemiologic primary exposure definition, but emphasizes that the data collection must not erase informal and day workers whose alert receipt cannot be verified through employer systems. She is particularly attentive to recruitment and documentation strategies that remain feasible without employer permission.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

meeting_opening: Start mid-thought, as if the conversation was already under way before the recording started.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: The meeting concerns one shared design step: determining the time at which a worker is considered exposed to a delayed smoke alert for the primary analysis. The environmental scientist proposes defining alert exposure using a county-level operational trigger: the earliest time during a shift when the relevant official PM2.5 alert is issued or the nearest regulatory monitor exceeds the pre-specified threshold, paired with forecast information only as a secondary descriptive measure. They say this produces a reproducible, independently verifiable time stamp for every worksite and avoids retrospectively inferring exposure from worker reports or uneven employer records. The epidemiologist proposes defining alert exposure from worker-level receipt and response: the time a participant reports receiving an alert or being told by a supervisor, corroborated where available by message logs, followed by a short exposure window based on actual work location and task. They say the study is about the intervention pathway, and a county trigger can misclassify workers who never received a warning, were indoors, changed tasks, or were already protected. The two proposals conflict because the primary analysis can use only one exposure-time definition. The sociologist explains that informal and day workers may receive alerts through supervisors, coworkers, family, Spanish-language networks, or not at all; asks that data collection record these pathways and any concern about losing shifts; and does not resolve the choice. Both primary-method proposals remain unresolved at the end of the meeting. No participant is asked to choose a winner or to provide a synthesis; the meeting should naturally surface each rationale and the specific bias or implementation problem it is intended to prevent.

ground_truth.shared_step: Define the timing of delayed-alert exposure for the study's primary analysis.

environmental_science_method.method: Use the earliest during-shift county-level official alert issuance or nearest regulatory-monitor PM2.5 threshold exceedance as the exposure time; retain plume forecasts as secondary descriptive information.
environmental_science_method.rationale: The time stamp is standardized, available for all worksites, and can be verified without relying on participant recall or incomplete workplace documentation.
environmental_science_method.problem_avoided: Avoids non-comparable, retrospective exposure timing based on worker reports and inconsistent employer records, as well as missing timing data for workers who cannot or do not report receipt.

epidemiology_method.method: Use the time the individual worker receives an alert or supervisor notification, supported by message logs when available, and analyze a short window using actual work location and task.
epidemiology_method.rationale: The relevant pathway for a protective-alert intervention is whether and when a worker actually receives actionable information and can alter exposure.
epidemiology_method.problem_avoided: Avoids misclassification from treating a county-wide environmental trigger as if every worker was notified, similarly exposed, outdoors, or unable to change task or location.

sociology_evidence.required_context: Alert receipt may occur through supervisors, coworkers, family, or language-specific community networks, and some informal or day workers may not receive an alert or may fear losing shifts if they request protections.
sociology_evidence.role_in_design: Collect alert source, language, employment arrangement, reported ability to respond, and concerns about lost work; this information explains unequal receipt and response but does not settle the primary exposure-time definition.

ground_truth.unresolved_decision: The meeting does not select either the operational county-trigger definition or the worker-level receipt-and-response definition as the primary analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …before we get into the timing definition, I hope everybody had a quieter weekend than the fire map suggested. For today, I'd like us to leave with a workable primary clock for the pilot. Are we timing from the county alert, from when a worker actually hears something, or some combination? I think that choice drives- it really drives almost everything in the follow-up design.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: …for the primary clock, I think we need something we can recover independently, even if a worker never gets a message or doesn’t want to report getting one. I’d use the earliest official county alert during the shift, or a pre-specified threshold crossing at the nearest regulatory monitor, and then treat receipt as a separate outcome. That doesn’t mean the monitor is their personal exposure, obviously. I still need to check whether monitor coverage is stable across the work corridors in both counties.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …right, but that clock tells us when the county condition began, not when the intervention could plausibly affect anyone. If receipt is only an outcome, we’ll call a worker nonresponsive even if they never saw the alert, or- if they heard it at dispatch an hour later. I’d keep the county trigger as the hazard anchor, absolutely, but I think primary follow-up should open at reported alert or supervisor communication, then we corroborate it where we can.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: …I worry that reported receipt kind of collapses a few different things. In interviews, people say they first heard about smoke through family or Spanish-language media, but they don't treat it as a workplace instruction until a foreperson says something. Could we record both, first awareness and first work-related communication, while keeping Maya's external trigger as the common hazard anchor? And for mobile crews, Maya, what geographic unit would that anchor use if they cross county— if they cross county lines?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …Lucía’s split is important. First awareness is context, but first work-related communication is the intervention receipt clock. And for crews crossing counties, I’d be careful not to let the anchor become a single county label. We should retain the alert and monitor conditions by their actual, um, location history, but that still shouldn’t substitute for whether anyone told them what to do.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: …for cross-county crews, I’d avoid assigning a single home county. We can geocode the reported work locations or route segments and apply the relevant county alert and nearest-monitor series over the shift, though I need to verify the monitor, the monitor density before I say that rule is stable. And I agree, the communication clocks should stay separate, first awareness versus an actual work-related instruction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: Mm, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …good. Then I’d make the questionnaire really explicit. “When did someone connected to your work first tell you about the smoke or ask you to do anything differently?” And we should allow in-person, group app, phone call, dispatcher, otherwise we recreate that problem where a missing text log looks like there was no communication.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: …and could we ask separately whether that communication came with a time they can actually place in the shift? I’m wondering, Rafael, in your mobile-worker work, how often do people have a message timestamp or screenshot versus just a later estimate, especially across job type or language. We can use either for the receipt outcome, but they’re not equivalent for the timing analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …it varied a lot, and I wouldn’t make a timestamp or screenshot a requirement for counting receipt. In the earlier cohort, quite a few people could place it in relation to the shift, like at dispatch, after lunch, when we got to the second site. But the exact clock time was fuzzy, especially with in-person and group-app communication. We can capture the source and how precise the timing is, then use a short window when they can credibly anchor it, instead of acting like every reported time has the same resolution.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: …that seems workable. On the environmental side, I’d want the same kind of precision flag. The nearest regulatory PM2.5 monitor gives us a recoverable crossing time, but the reported site or route segment may only be known to, say, a morning versus afternoon location. So we should probably keep both rather than force a minute-level, I mean minute-by-minute comparison that the inputs can’t support.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Exactly. We can make timing precision an analytic variable instead of a reason to throw out the event. We can code it as clock time, a shift-anchored estimate, or just a broad period. The short response window can- we can define that around the precision, so it’s tighter after a timestamped message and broader when it was "at the second site." But I’d still want the work location and task change recorded at that point, not just the county conditions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: …and I wouldn't assume that first work-related message came from management. It could be a coworker passing something along from a Spanish-language WhatsApp group or radio, in a group conversation, and people may only place it as “before lunch” or “at the second site.” We should record who conveyed it, the channel, and the language, but keep that separate from whether any instruction or protective option followed.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: The separation is right. For the primary clock, I'd count the first work-connected communication as receipt, whether that came from a supervisor or a coworker. But then the next link is- we need to code that separately. Was there an instruction, an option like shade, respirator, reassignment, stopping, and could they actually use it? Otherwise we'll confuse being informed with having any real opportunity to respond.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: Right, and language too.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah—language and channel need to be part of the receipt record, not an afterthought.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: …yes, and I’d make Spanish-language networks a named response category instead of burying them under “other” — radio, WhatsApp groups, family messages, worker organizations. The same person may have early community awareness in Spanish and then a different, later workplace message in English or from a foreperson. That difference may matter for whether they felt able to act.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …and that gives us a useful sequence instead of one overloaded “alert received” field. Community awareness, then work-connected communication, then an instruction or a usable option. We should ask whether that later workplace message changed anything from what they already knew. Otherwise, a worker who heard it on WhatsApp at ten and gets no accommodation at noon can artificially look like they had the same intervention as somebody whose foreperson actually reassigned them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: …and we should ask whether they felt they could actually use that option without losing hours, a future shift, or being seen as difficult. Otherwise, otherwise, “respirator offered” or “reassignment mentioned” can look available in the data when, especially for a day worker, it was not practically usable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I’d treat practical usability as part of the intervention, not just something we modify afterward. In the follow-up, we can ask very concretely, after you heard this, could you take the option without losing pay, being sent home, or risking the next shift? And if not, what made it unavailable? That separates an offer on paper from an actionable, um, response.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: Yes—otherwise availability is being measured, not a worker’s actual room to act.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hm, yes, practically usable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Yeah—usable, in the worker’s actual circumstances, is the measure we need.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lucía Benítez
transcript.text: I think we have what we needed for today. Thank you both, this has been very, very helpful, and we can pick up the remaining details next time.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Thanks, this was really useful. Bye.
